# Introduction

This guide provides you with:

1. a detailed outline of course content;
2. sources for content; and
3. where to find the most relevant practice material.

This release covers the first four weeks of the regression section.
Later weeks
will be added to the rendered document as they are taught.
The main regression
notes, `NotesReg.pdf`, remain a key source throughout and should be used
alongside the slides and practice material.

::: {.callout-important title="Disclaimer"}
Whilst this document is detailed, its intention is not to be absolutely exhaustive.
In general, the course outline, notes, slides, what we discuss in class and any practice material define the boundaries of what is examinable.
If you are unsure whether a topic is examinable, please ask.
:::

## Recommended study route

After each lecture or slide deck:

1. Review the relevant section of the slides and notes.
2. Complete the matching Q&A document to check factual understanding.
3. Work through the relevant tutorial questions.
4. Work through the relevant practical questions, which also assist in practising the theory.
5. Use the question bank for additional practice.
6. If time, work through any past papers.

The Q&A documents are primarily for recall and understanding.
Tutorials,
question-bank questions, practicals and past assessments provide more sustained
problem-solving practice.
Past papers may be useful, but I try to make the other practice material as comprehensive as possible.

## Weekly overview

| Week | Main theme | Main objective |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Introduction, prerequisites and the multivariate normal distribution | Understand what regression is for and master the probability and linear-algebra results used in later regression derivations. |
| 2 | The general linear model | Formulate the model in matrix form, estimate its parameters, and derive the principal sampling distributions. |
| 3 | Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests | Use the sampling distributions from Week 2 to quantify uncertainty and test hypotheses about regression effects. |
| 4 | ANOVA and model checking | Relate ANOVA to regression, handle categorical explanatory variables, and assess whether a fitted linear model is adequate. |

# Proofs and derivations

The proofs below are not separate from the rest of the course.
You should know
what each result says, why its assumptions matter, and how the result is used in
later regression arguments.

## Week 1

In `SlidesRegW1S3MVN.pdf`:

- a linear transformation of a multivariate normal random vector is
  multivariate normal;
- a selected component or partition of a multivariate normal random vector is
  multivariate normal;
- if $\mathbf Z\sim N_k(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)$ and $\mathbf A$ is symmetric and
  idempotent, then

  $$
  \mathbf Z^T\mathbf A\mathbf Z
  \sim \chi^2_{\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf A)}.
  $$

## Week 2

In `2. General linear models/Notes/NotesRegW2GLM.pdf`:

- derivation of the least-squares estimator

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
  =(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf Y.
  $$

In `Proofs/Notes/slides/NotesRegProofs.pdf` and the accompanying
proof-specific slides in `Proofs/Notes/slides`:

- why the least-squares estimator is also the maximum-likelihood estimator under normally distributed errors;
- derivation of the distribution of $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$;
- derivation of the maximum-likelihood estimator of $\sigma^2$;
- bias of $\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ and unbiasedness of
  $s^2=\mathrm{SSE}/(n-k)$;
- derivation of

  $$
  \frac{(n-k)s^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-k};
  $$

- a useful alternative expression for $s^2$.

## Week 3

In `Proofs/Notes/slides/NotesRegProofs.pdf`:

- independence of a linear form and a quadratic form of a multivariate normal
  random vector, under the stated conditions;
- independence of $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and $s^2$.

In `SlidesRegW3S1ConfInt.pdf`:

- derivation of the $t$-distributed pivot used for inference about a single
  linear combination $\boldsymbol\ell^T\boldsymbol\beta$.

In `SlidesRegW3S2HypTestV2.pdf`:

- derivation of the $t$ statistic for testing a single linear combination of
  coefficients;
- derivation of the $F$ statistic for testing several linear combinations
  simultaneously.

## Week 4

In `SlidesRegW4L2ModelChecking.pdf`:

- the joint distribution of the residauls

- the result $\sum_i h_i=k$, and hence average leverage $k/n$.

# Week 1: Introduction and multivariate normal foundations

## What you need to know

### Purpose and scope of regression

You should understand:

- the roles of the response variable, explanatory variables and random error;
- what a regression model provides beyond an overall mean, a correlation
  coefficient or a two-sample comparison;
- the distinction between simple and multiple linear regression;
- the main assumptions of a linear regression model at a conceptual level

### Statistical-distribution prerequisites

You should be able to move between the normal, chi-squared, $t$ and $F$
distributions.

### Linear-algebra prerequisites

You should be comfortable with:

- matrix dimensions, rows, columns, transposes and multiplication;
- block matrices and block-matrix multiplication;
- orthogonality and orthonormality;
- trace, including the cyclic trace property;
- rank, full column/row rank and linear dependence;
- invertibility;
- eigenvalues and eigenvectors;
- symmetric, positive-definite, positive-semidefinite and idempotent matrices;
- orthonormal eigendecompositions of symmetric matrices;
- the fact that the eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix are zero or one.

### The multivariate normal distribution

You should know and be able to use:

- the univariate and multivariate normal density functions;
- the mean vector and variance-covariance matrix of a multivariate normal random
  vector;
- the moment-generating function of a multivariate normal random vector;
- the theorem for a linear transformation

  $$
  \mathbf Y=\mathbf A\mathbf X+\mathbf b;
  $$

- selection matrices for extracting individual components and subvectors;
- the result that partitions and marginal subvectors of a multivariate normal
  random vector are themselves multivariate normal;
- chi-squared quadratic-form results, including

  $$
  (\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)^T
  \boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}
  (\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)
  \sim\chi^2_p
  $$

  when $\mathbf X\sim N_p(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)$ with invertible
  $\boldsymbol\Sigma$;
- the symmetric-idempotent quadratic-form theorem stated in the proofs section.

::: {.callout-note title="What is not required for assessment"}
You are not required to derive the multivariate normal density, derive its MGF,
or determine the mean and covariance matrix by manipulating the exponent of an
MVN density.
You must nevertheless be able to **state and use** the density, MGF
and associated theorems.
:::

# Week 2: The general linear model

## What you need to know

### Model formulation

The general linear model is

$$
\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon,
$$

where $\mathbf Y$ is an $n\times1$ response vector, $\mathbf X$ is a fixed
$n\times k$ design matrix, $\boldsymbol\beta$ is a $k\times1$ parameter vector,
and $\boldsymbol\epsilon$ is an $n\times1$ random error vector.

You should understand:

- scalar, vector and matrix representations of the same model;
- which quantities are observed, fixed, unknown or random;
- the role of the intercept column;
- how numerical explanatory variables enter the design matrix;
- the assumptions

  $$
  \operatorname E(\boldsymbol\epsilon)=\mathbf 0,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\epsilon)=\sigma^2\mathbf I;
  $$

- the additional normality assumption when exact finite-sample distributions
  are required;
- why $\mathbf X$ must have full column rank and why $n>k$;
- simple and multiple linear regression as special cases.

### Estimating the regression coefficients

You should know:

- ordinary least squares as minimisation of

  $$
  \operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)
  =(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^T
   (\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta);
  $$

- the normal equations;
- the estimator

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
  =(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf Y;
  $$

- why normality is not needed to obtain the least-squares formula;
- why the same estimator is the MLE under normal errors;
- unbiasedness and the variance-covariance matrix of the estimator;
- under normal errors,

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
  \sim
  N_k\left(
    \boldsymbol\beta,
    \sigma^2(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}
  \right);
  $$

- distributions of individual coefficients and linear functions such as
  $\boldsymbol\ell^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and
  $\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$;
- how the scale and mutual correlation of explanatory variables affect the
  precision and covariance of coefficient estimators.

### Fitted values, residuals and residual variance

You should know:

- fitted values

  $$
  \hat{\mathbf Y}=\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta};
  $$

- residuals

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}
  =\mathbf Y-\hat{\mathbf Y};
  $$

- the difference between an unobserved error and an observed residual;
- the hat matrix

  $$
  \mathbf H
  =\mathbf X(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T;
  $$

- the residual-maker matrix $\mathbf M=\mathbf I-\mathbf H$ and the projection
  interpretation of $\mathbf H\mathbf Y$ and $\mathbf M\mathbf Y$;
- the residual sum of squares and the estimators

  $$
  \hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}
  =\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n},
  \qquad
  s^2=\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-k};
  $$

- why the MLE is biased, why $s^2$ is unbiased, and the role of residual degrees
  of freedom;
- the chi-squared distribution of the scaled unbiased variance estimator.

### Interpretation

A coefficient in a multiple regression model describes the change in the
conditional mean response associated with a one-unit increase in its
explanatory variable, **holding the other explanatory variables fixed**.
The interpretation must include the units, the comparison and the fact that it is a
mean effect under the model.

# Week 3: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests

## What you need to know

### Why we need inference

The estimates from Week 2 vary from sample to sample.
You should understand the distinction between:

- a point estimate, which gives one estimated value;
- a confidence interval, which describes the values compatible with the data
  and model at a stated confidence level;
- a hypothesis test, which asks whether the data provide enough evidence to
  reject a specified null hypothesis.

For inference about the regression coefficients, write

$$
\mathbf C=(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}.
$$

You should know that

$$
\boldsymbol\ell^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
\sim
N\left(
  \boldsymbol\ell^T\boldsymbol\beta,
  \sigma^2\boldsymbol\ell^T\mathbf C\boldsymbol\ell
\right)
$$

for any fixed vector $\boldsymbol\ell$ of the appropriate length.
You should also know why replacing the unknown $\sigma^2$ by $s^2$ means that
we use a $t$ rather than a normal distribution for exact finite-sample
inference under the normal-error model.

The key result is

$$
\frac{
  \boldsymbol\ell^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
  -\boldsymbol\ell^T\boldsymbol\beta
}{
  s\sqrt{\boldsymbol\ell^T\mathbf C\boldsymbol\ell}
}
\sim t_{n-k}.
$$

This uses the Week 2 chi-squared result for $s^2$ together with the independence
of $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and $s^2$.

### Confidence intervals

You should be able to construct and interpret the $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence
interval

$$
\boldsymbol\ell^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
\pm
t_{n-k}^{1-\alpha/2}
s\sqrt{\boldsymbol\ell^T\mathbf C\boldsymbol\ell}.
$$

Important special cases include:

- an individual regression coefficient;
- a difference or other linear combination of coefficients;
- the conditional mean response at specified explanatory-variable values,
  obtained by setting $\boldsymbol\ell$ equal to the relevant design row.

You should be able to move between a substantive comparison and the required
$\boldsymbol\ell$ vector.
You should also be able to calculate a confidence interval from R output or
from the quantities in the formula above.

For interpretation and reporting, you should understand:

- what it means for zero to lie inside or outside a coefficient confidence
  interval;
- what it means for a confidence interval to contain, or not contain, negligible or practically important values;
- that the interval concerns the uncertainty in the estimated mean response or
  regression effect, not the spread of individual future observations.

### Nominal and empirical coverage

You should understand the difference between nominal and empirical coverage.
In particular, you should be able to explain why simply inserting $s$ into a
normal-based interval gives intervals that are too narrow in small samples,
and why the $t$ interval corrects for the extra uncertainty from estimating
$\sigma^2$.

### Hypothesis tests for one linear combination

For a null hypothesis of the form

$$
H_0:\boldsymbol\ell^T\boldsymbol\beta=c,
$$

you should be able to use

$$
t=
\frac{
  \boldsymbol\ell^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-c
}{
  s\sqrt{\boldsymbol\ell^T\mathbf C\boldsymbol\ell}
}
\sim t_{n-k}
$$

under $H_0$.

You should be able to:

- state the null and alternative hypotheses;
- calculate the test statistic and its degrees of freedom;
- calculate or obtain the p-value for a one-sided or two-sided test;
- make the test decision at a stated significance level;
- relate a two-sided test to the corresponding confidence interval.

An individual coefficient test is a special case obtained by choosing
$\boldsymbol\ell$ to select that coefficient.
You should also be able to test comparisons such as the difference between two
regression coefficients.

### Hypothesis tests for several linear combinations

Some questions involve several restrictions at once. Write these as

$$
H_0:\mathbf L\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf c,
$$

where $\mathbf L$ has $q$ linearly independent rows.
You should know the test statistic

$$
F=
\frac{
  (\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf c)^T
  (\mathbf L\mathbf C\mathbf L^T)^{-1}
  (\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf c)
}{q s^2}
\sim F_{q,n-k}
$$

under $H_0$.

You should be able to construct $\mathbf L$ for the stated hypothesis and use
the resulting $F$ statistic. This includes tests that several specified
coefficients are zero, including the usual test that all slope coefficients
are zero.
Separate $t$ tests do not answer the same joint question.

### Interpretation and reporting

You should understand that:

- a small p-value is evidence against the null hypothesis, under the model;
- a p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true;
- a large p-value does not establish that the effect is zero;
- the estimated effect and its uncertainty matter as well as statistical
  significance;
- statistical significance does not by itself imply a practically important
  effect.

When reporting a regression effect, state the effect in context and give its
uncertainty. For a multiple regression coefficient, make clear that the
comparison holds the other explanatory variables fixed.

# Week 4: ANOVA and model checking

## What you need to know

### One-way ANOVA

Given the one-way model

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu+\alpha_i+e_{ij},
$$

you should be able to state the equal-means null hypothesis. Know the test statistic

$$
F
=
\frac{SS_A/(a-1)}{SSE/(n-a)}
=
\frac{MS_A}{MSE}
\sim F_{a-1,n-a}
$$

under the null hypothesis.

I won't ask you to read an ANOVA table.

### Categorical explanatory variables in regression

A categorical explanatory variable with $a$ levels can be represented in a
regression model using indicator variables. You should understand:

- why fitting an intercept and one indicator for every level makes the columns
  of the design matrix linearly dependent;
- why reference coding uses $a-1$ indicator variables when an intercept is
  present;
- how to identify the reference level from the model specification or output;
- how to construct the corresponding rows of the design matrix;
- that the intercept is the mean for the reference level when the other
  explanatory variables are zero;
- that each category coefficient is a difference from the reference level,
  holding any other explanatory variables fixed.
- how to change the reference level by adjusting the design matrix.
- that a simultaneous hypothesis test is required when there are more than two levels to test whether a given factor has an effect on the response.

### ANOVA as regression and the joint $F$ test

For a reference-coded one-way ANOVA, equality of all group means is equivalent
to testing that all $a-1$ category coefficients are zero. Write this as

$$
H_0:\mathbf L\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0,
$$

where $\mathbf L$ selects the category coefficients.

You should understand that the same one-way ANOVA hypothesis can be tested in
three equivalent ways:

1. directly using $SS_A$ and $SSE$;
2. using the general $\mathbf L\boldsymbol\beta$ regression $F$ test from Week
   3; or
3. by comparing a reduced and an unrestricted model.

For nested reduced and unrestricted models, know

$$
F
=
\frac{
  (SSE_R-SSE_{UR})/(k_{UR}-k_R)
}{
  SSE_{UR}/(n-k_{UR})
}
\sim
F_{k_{UR}-k_R,\,n-k_{UR}}
$$

under the null hypothesis.

You should be able to construct the reduced and unrestricted models for a
stated hypothesis.

You should also know that the overall $F$ statistic in `summary(lm(...))` tests
whether all non-intercept coefficients are zero.

### Two-way ANOVA and order of terms

You do not need to know this part of the slides.

### $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$

For a least-squares model with an intercept,

$$
R^2
=
\frac{SSR}{SST}
=
1-\frac{SSE}{SST}.
$$

You should understand $R^2$ as the proportion of the observed variation in the
response explained by the fitted regression. You should also know that adding
explanatory variables cannot reduce $R^2$.

You do not need to know that calculation formula on slide 5.

Adjusted $R^2$ is

$$
R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}
=
1-
\frac{SSE/(n-k)}{SST/(n-1)}
=
1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-k}.
$$

It penalises the addition of regression parameters and can decrease when a weak
term is added. Neither $R^2$ nor adjusted $R^2$ replaces checking whether the
model assumptions are plausible.

### Model assumptions and graphical checks

- Why we use residuals rather than errors (errors are unobserved)
- What model assumptions we actually need to check

You should be
able to use:

- a residuals-versus-fitted plot to look for a systematic mean pattern and
  non-constant spread;
- a histogram or density plot of residuals to look for strong skewness or
  unusual tails;
- a normal Q-Q plot, which should be approximately linear when normality is a
  reasonable approximation (and to interpret the bands as a rough guide to sampling variability);
- the Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests as formal checks of normality (and that SW is more sensitive than KS, and that both are sensitive to sample size);,
  including stating the null hypothesis and interpreting the p-value.

Graphical and formal checks should be considered together.\
A formal test does
not tell you whether a deviation is important for the analysis by itsel.

### Residuals and outliers

- Know the distribution of the residuals.
- Distinguish between raw residuals, internally studentised residuals and externally studentised residuals.
- Formulae for internally and externally studentised residuals, and how to convert from internally to externally studentised residuals.
- You do not need to know the distribution of the externally-studentised residauls, nor do you need to know how to derive the shortcut in working out the externally studentised residuals with one model fit (just that you can do it, and what the formula is). You also do not need to knwo thresholds.
- What the difference fundamentally is between internally and externally studentised residuals, and why and when that matters.
- How to practically handle large outliers
- How to interpret a plot of studentised residuals against index

### Leverage and influential observations

- Difference between outliers and high-leverage points.
- Definition of leverage
- That leverage is the extent to which an observation predicts itself
- Why high leverage tends to reduce the residual
- Cook-type diagnostics combine residual size and leverage (do not need to know their formulae; you do not have to remember anything about the modified Cook's distance, and I also won't ask you about Cook's distance that uses s^2 estimated without the current observation)
- How to practically handle large leverage points
- How to interpret a plot of leverage/Cook's distance against index

# Week 5: Matching the model to the data

## Transformations and additional model terms

### Content

- Why the original linear model may not match the data:
  - non-linearity;
  - non-constant variance;
  - skewness;
  - outliers;
  - missing effect modification.
- Transforming the response:
  - common log and square-root transformations;
  - linearising relationships;
  - stabilising variance;
  - reducing skewness and the impact of extreme observations;
  - consequences for every explanatory-variable relationship;
  - interpretation on the transformed and original scales.
- Transforming an explanatory variable:
  - log, square-root, exponential and square transformations;
  - correcting a specific non-linear relationship;
  - why this does not itself fix non-constant residual variance;
  - interpretation after transforming $X$.
- Introducing new explanatory variables:
  - polynomial terms;
  - discretised versions of a numerical variable;
  - interactions.
- Interactions between a numerical and a categorical explanatory variable:
  - model formula;
  - design matrix;
  - fitted lines for each group;
  - group-specific intercepts and slopes;
  - differences between groups at a specified value of $X$;
  - two-level and multi-level factors.
- Tests involving interactions:
  - whether slopes differ across groups;
  - whether $X$ has an effect within a specified group;
  - whether $X$ has an effect in any group;
  - whether groups differ at a specified value of $X$;
  - whether a factor has any effect through either intercepts or slopes.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- diagnose which aspect of a model a transformation is intended to address;
- decide whether transforming $Y$, transforming an $X$, or adding model terms
  is the more targeted response;
- interpret coefficients on transformed scales and describe the corresponding
  relationship on the original scale;
- construct the design matrix for polynomial and interaction models;
- calculate and plot fitted values for every level of an interacting factor;
- interpret main effects in the presence of an interaction;
- calculate group-specific slopes and between-group differences;
- express each substantive interaction question as one or several linear
  restrictions and choose a $t$ or $F$ test accordingly;
- re-check the model after modifying its structure.

## Prediction, variable selection and model performance

### Content

- Conditional mean versus an individual future response.
- Confidence interval for a mean response versus prediction interval for a new
  observation.
- Sources of variability in each interval.
- Prediction interval:

  $$
  \hat{Y}_f
  \pm
  t_{n-k}^{1-\alpha/2}
  s\sqrt{
    1+\mathbf{x}_f'
    (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
    \mathbf{x}_f
  }.
  $$

- Why prediction intervals are wider than confidence intervals.
- What happens to each interval as sample size grows.
- Why interval bands widen away from the centre of the observed design.
- Motivation for variable selection:
  - interpretation;
  - cost of measurement;
  - prediction accuracy;
  - bias-variance trade-off.
- Why exhaustive search is often infeasible.
- Algorithms:
  - forward selection;
  - backward elimination;
  - stepwise selection.
- Selection criteria:
  - AIC;
  - BIC;
  - adjusted $R^2$;
  - balancing fit against model complexity.
- How the AIC and BIC penalties differ as sample size changes.
- Limitations of greedy selection algorithms.
- Why ordinary p-values are not trustworthy after data-driven variable
  selection without accounting for the selection process.
- Training and test data:
  - evaluating prediction on unseen observations;
  - optimism of training error;
  - trade-off in choosing the split size;
  - uncertainty in the fitted model versus uncertainty in estimated test error.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- derive and calculate a prediction interval;
- explain every source of uncertainty in a confidence or prediction interval;
- choose the interval appropriate to an applied decision;
- describe forward, backward and stepwise selection and identify when each can
  or cannot be run;
- calculate and compare AIC and BIC values;
- explain why a criterion may favour a larger or smaller model;
- critique inferential claims made after model selection;
- design a training-test split and explain its competing sources of
  uncertainty;
- evaluate predictive performance on unseen data.

## Gauss-Markov theorem

### Content

- Statement and assumptions of the theorem.
- Meaning of each word in BLUE:
  - best;
  - linear;
  - unbiased;
  - estimator.
- Proof that OLS has the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators.
- Normality is not required for the Gauss-Markov result.
- Difference between:
  - OLS being BLUE;
  - OLS being maximum likelihood;
  - exact normal-theory confidence intervals and tests being valid.
- Consequences of:
  - omitted variables correlated with included variables;
  - non-linearity in the parameters;
  - non-constant variance;
  - correlated errors;
  - biased estimators with smaller variance.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- state the Gauss-Markov theorem precisely;
- identify which assumptions are needed and which are not;
- explain the comparison class implicit in the word "best";
- reproduce the proof and explain why the added covariance term is
  non-negative;
- determine whether the theorem applies to a proposed model;
- distinguish low variance from low mean-squared error when bias is present;
- explain why satisfying the theorem does not establish that a model is
  scientifically adequate.

# Week 6: Bootstrapping and principal components analysis

## Bootstrapping

### Content

- Sampling distributions and why they are needed for inference.
- Limitations of normal and $t$ approximations when the sampling distribution
  is skewed or otherwise poorly approximated.
- The central idea of the non-parametric bootstrap:
  - treat the empirical distribution as an estimate of the population
    distribution;
  - sample observations with replacement;
  - keep each bootstrap sample the same size as the original sample;
  - recompute the statistic for many bootstrap samples.
- Why sampling with replacement is essential.
- Bootstrap estimate of a sampling distribution and standard error.
- Bootstrap confidence intervals:
  - percentile interval;
  - interval using a bootstrap standard error and a theoretical $t$ quantile;
  - bootstrap-$t$ interval.
- Which intervals can be asymmetric and where the asymmetry arises.
- Comparing bootstrap methods with ordinary normal and $t$ intervals.
- Strengths and limitations:
  - fewer parametric assumptions;
  - dependence on the observed sample being representative;
  - difficulty with very small samples, dependent observations or inappropriate
    resampling units;
  - simulation error and the number of bootstrap repetitions.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- explain sampling with replacement and construct a bootstrap sample;
- distinguish a data distribution from a statistic's sampling distribution;
- describe the bootstrap algorithm in words, notation and R;
- estimate a bootstrap standard error;
- calculate or interpret percentile, bootstrap-standard-error and bootstrap-$t$
  intervals;
- identify which interval methods allow asymmetry;
- explain when a bootstrap method may improve on a theoretical approximation;
- identify settings in which a naive bootstrap would be unreliable.

## Principal components analysis

### Content

- Purposes of PCA:
  - dimensionality reduction;
  - visualisation;
  - pattern recognition;
  - noise reduction;
  - reducing collinearity among derived explanatory variables.
- Centring and, where appropriate, standardising the original variables.
- Covariance-matrix versus correlation-matrix PCA.
- Definition of a principal component as a linear combination of the original
  variables.
- Loading vectors and the unit-length constraint.
- Principal-component scores.
- Variance-maximising objective and orthogonality constraints.
- Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix as loading vectors.
- Eigenvalues as component variances.
- Ordering of components and why components are uncorrelated.
- Total variance and proportion of variance explained:

  $$
  \operatorname{PVE}_j
  =\frac{\lambda_j}{\sum_{r=1}^p\lambda_r},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{CPVE}_m
  =\frac{\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j}{\sum_{r=1}^p\lambda_r}.
  $$

- Choosing the number of components:
  - scree plot and elbow;
  - cumulative proportion of variance explained;
  - interpretability and the aim of the analysis.
- Interpreting loadings:
  - magnitude;
  - sign;
  - contrasts and shared patterns among variables;
  - arbitrary reversal of a component's sign.
- Consequences of a covariance matrix that is not full rank.
- Regression using principal-component scores and the resulting coefficient
  correlations.
- Costs and limitations:
  - information loss;
  - difficult interpretation;
  - sensitivity to scale;
  - high variance need not mean high relevance to a response.
- Reading and interpreting the main output of `prcomp()`.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- explain why PCA is used and when standardisation is necessary;
- calculate a covariance matrix and its eigendecomposition;
- identify the loading vector and variance of each component;
- calculate principal-component scores for specified observations;
- prove or explain why component variances are eigenvalues and components are
  uncorrelated;
- calculate total, individual and cumulative proportions of variance
  explained;
- draw and interpret a scree plot;
- motivate the number of components retained using more than one criterion;
- interpret a component from its loadings while recognising sign ambiguity;
- explain the effect of rank deficiency;
- relate PCA to regression with correlated explanatory variables;
- critique the claim that the last components are necessarily irrelevant.

# Statistical computing and applied analysis

The practical strand is cumulative. A later assessment may require earlier R
and data-analysis skills even when its statistical topic comes from a later
week.

| Practical stage | Competencies |
|---|---|
| Data preparation and exploration | Load and inspect data; calculate summaries; distinguish numerical, nominal and ordinal variables; create histograms, densities, boxplots, scatterplots and pairwise plots; identify skewness, outliers and possible collinearity. |
| Model formulation and fitting | Simulate data; create factors with appropriate levels; construct model and design matrices; fit simple, multiple, categorical, transformed and interaction models; calculate OLS estimates manually. |
| Inference | Extract model components; calculate standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values and nested-model tests; distinguish individual and simultaneous hypotheses. |
| Programming foundations | Work with vectors and matrices; write `for` loops; use conditions and `if`, `else` and `ifelse`; distinguish scalar and element-wise logical operators; write and debug functions. |
| Simulation | Estimate coverage and power; keep fixed and random quantities distinct; repeat an analysis reproducibly; summarise and plot simulation results. |
| Model assessment | Calculate ANOVA components; obtain fitted values and residual diagnostics; identify outliers, leverage and influence; compare training and test performance. |
| Communication | State the analytical goal; justify model choices; interpret effects in context; report uncertainty; distinguish statistical from practical importance; present reproducible code and clear tables and figures. |

The [previous practicals](../_reference/eval/2025/) and
[previous assignment](../_reference/eval/2025/AssignmentRegQuestions.qmd)
show how these competencies can be combined in longer applied questions.

# Final revision checklist

Before an assessment, check that you can do each of the following without
depending on a memorised example:

- translate a substantive question into a model and one or more hypotheses;
- construct the relevant design row, contrast vector or contrast matrix;
- calculate an estimate, standard error, interval or test statistic;
- state the assumptions behind the calculation;
- interpret the result in the units and context of the problem;
- identify what the result does not establish;
- use diagnostic evidence to assess the model;
- connect the mathematics to the corresponding R output;
- reproduce the required proofs and adapt the underlying results to a new
  derivation.
